newsitem.title: CHILE: Leaders arrive for Chilean summit on democracy.
newsitem.headline: Leaders arrive for Chilean summit on democracy.

text.p: The leaders of 19 Latin American nations plus Spain and Portugal began arriving in Chile on Saturday for an Ibero-American summit whose official theme is how to get Latin Americans to care about democracy.

Cuban President Fidel Castro, in his first visit to Chile since the turbulent early 1970s, set aside his usual military fatigues and arrived in a blue business suit for the summit on raising citizens' participation in democracy.
"I express my satisfaction on returning to this extraordinary country which I visited exactly 25 years ago," said Castro in a brief arrival statement.
"I wish you well-being and peace," he said after being met by Chilean Economy Minister Alvaro Garcia.

With Chilean President Eduardo Frei playing host, Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, the king and queen of Spain and the prime ministers of Spain and Portugal, among others, all arrived for the sixth Ibero-American Summit.

Police blocked car and pedestrian traffic along the leaders' route to their hotel, preventing Castro's admirers and opponents from demonstrating along his motorcade route as they had planned. Tight security prevented street rallies.
The official theme of the summit -- "Governability in an Efficient and Participative Democracy" -- may sound more like an issue for a sociologists' convention than a meeting of presidents.

But Chilean officials, who picked the theme, insisted it had relevance in a region where almost everyone lives in democracy but many do not bother to vote, do not care about politics and may not even care if they live under dictatorship or democracy.
"What does governability mean? It means building a better, more participative government, within reach of its citizens and at the service of the community," Frei said.
Some leaders tried to dispel the idea that such summits were nothing more than photo ops and high-level hobnobbing.
"We've come for some days of very intense work, bearing in mind the common interests of our countries and our citizens," said Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar.

Most of Latin America returned to democratic rule in the 1980s after long spells of dictatorship, in processes that resembled moves to democracy in Spain and Portugal in the 1970s. Chile was among the last, restoring civilian rule in 1990.

"Generally at these summits, people talk about economic and social development. This is the first summit of any kind in which we'll be talking about political development," said the summit's chief organiser, Fabio Vio.

The annual Ibero-American summits began in Guadalajara, Mexico, in 1991 as a way of cementing closer economic and cultural ties between Latin America and its former colonial masters Spain and Portugal.
Diplomats said the meeting's final document had been drafted and would be put to the presidents for their review, and then released at the end of the summit on Monday.
The document made no call, either directly or indirectly, for any democratic reforms in Cuba, the one country represented at the summit without an elected government, diplomats said.

"The document cannot make any reference to a specific country without consensus, and that consensus must include the country in question," said Chilean Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza, asked about references to Cuba.
Other diplomats said the Spanish delegation pressed for some kind of call for reform to Cuba's one-party system without mentioning Cuba by name, but Mexico led opposition to any such reference.

But the document did criticise the Helms-Burton Act tightening the U.S. embargo on Cuba, diplomats said, in another victory for Castro against the law that was lambasted by Washington's allies in Europe and the Americas.
